meta.title: It is my film: Yojimbo and A Fistful of Dollars
meta.angle: a work and its remake, and the lawsuit between them

candide.instructions: A curious, quick podcast co-host. Warm, informal, genuinely asking, a little impatient. Natural pace, light tone.

expert.instructions: A calm, precise film expert. Unhurried, slightly amused, never lecturing. Quotations are read a touch slower, as if reading from the page.

beats.text: Two films, three years apart. A nameless samurai walks into a town at war with itself. A nameless gunman does exactly the same. And one director wrote the other a letter.
Let's get it out of the way. Leone copied Kurosawa. End of story?

Here is the letter, in full. Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film, but it is my film. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright, you must pay me.

source.quote: Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film, but it is my film. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright, you must pay me.

brick.text: It is a very fine film, but it is my film.

beats.text: That is a lawyer's letter. Did he pay?

Toho sued. Leone ignored the lawsuit, then settled out of court: fifteen percent of the worldwide receipts and over one hundred thousand dollars. Kurosawa earned more money from this settlement than from Yojimbo.

source.quote: Leone ignored the resulting lawsuit, but eventually settled out of court, reportedly for 15% of the worldwide receipts of A Fistful of Dollars and over $100,000.
Kurosawa earned more money from this settlement than from Yojimbo.

beats.text: More from the lawsuit than from his own film?
The film cost two hundred thousand dollars. It sold nearly fifteen million tickets in Italy alone and grossed more than nineteen point nine million dollars worldwide.

source.quote: It sold admissions of 14,797,275 ticket sales in Italy.
totaling more than $19.9 million grossed worldwide

beats.text: How did it even get released?

Badly. No major distributor wanted a faux-Western by an unknown director, so it came out in Italy on the twelfth of September 1964, typically the worst month for sales, and the Italian critics shunned it. It spread at a grassroots level and ended at 2.7 billion lire, more than any other Italian film to that point.

source.quote: The film ended up being released in Italy 12 September 1964, which was typically the worst month for sales.
it grossed 2.7 billion lire ($4,375,000) in Italy, more than any other Italian film to that point.
The film was initially shunned by Italian critics, who gave it extremely negative reviews.

beats.text: And it hid its accent. Few spaghetti Westerns had reached the United States, so the Europeans took American-sounding names: Leone became Bob Robertson, Gian Maria Volonté became Johnny Wels, and the composer Ennio Morricone, Dan Savio. It was shot in Spain, mostly near Hoyo de Manzanares close to Madrid, and in the Tabernas Desert of Almería.

source.quote: These included Leone ("Bob Robertson"), Gian Maria Volonté ("Johnny Wels") and the composer, Ennio Morricone ("Dan Savio").
A Fistful of Dollars was shot in Spain, mostly near Hoyo de Manzanares close to Madrid

brick.caption: Bob Robertson · Johnny Wels · Dan Savio

beats.text: Bob Robertson. Right.
Fine. But was it really a copy, or just the same kind of story?
Same opening. An innkeeper explains the war to the stranger: Gonji, with the bosses Ushitora and Seibei; Silvanito, with the Rojos and the Baxters.

source.quote: The owner Gonji advises the rōnin to leave, and tells him that the two warring bosses, Ushitora and Seibei, are fighting over the lucrative gambling trade run by Seibei.
Silvanito, the town's innkeeper, tells the Stranger about a feud between two smuggler families vying to gain control of the town

source.line: The Baxters on one side. The Rojos on the other.

brick.caption: “The Baxters on one side. The Rojos on the other.” (00:31:56)

beats.text: Same demonstration: the samurai kills three of Ushitora's men to get hired, the gunman shoots the four men who insulted him on his way in.

source.quote: He demonstrates his deadliness to both sides by shooting to death with ease the four men who insulted him as he entered town.

beats.text: And the coffin maker counts. On his way to the fight, Sanjuro orders two coffins, then corrects himself: no, better make that three. In San Miguel the stranger tells the coffin maker to get three coffins ready, and comes back with: my mistake, four coffins.
Same joke, one more body.
One more body. Leone keeps the joke and raises the count. That is the whole film in one line.
And the names? The samurai has one, doesn't he?

He makes one up, looking at a mulberry field: Kuwabatake Sanjuro, mulberry field, thirty years old. The sheet calls him an early man with no name. Leone's stranger gets even less: the sheet only ever calls him the Stranger, and one line of the film calls him Joe.

source.quote: When asked his name, the samurai calls himself "Kuwabatake Sanjuro", which he seems to make up while looking at a mulberry field by the town.
An unnamed stranger arrives at the little frontier town of San Miguel.

source.line: Joe, I have prepared the wagon

beats.text: Then the beats line up. A lie planted in both camps. A woman handed over for a debt, Nui or Marisol, freed and sent away with money. The hero found out, beaten, escaping in a coffin, and coming back because the innkeeper has been taken.

The woman first. In Yojimbo she is Nui, a farmer's wife: her husband sold her to Ushitora to settle a gambling debt, and Ushitora gave her to the brewer Tokuemon as chattel to gain his support. In Fistful she is Marisol: Ramón accused her husband Julio of cheating at cards and took her as collateral.

source.quote: Sanjuro learns that the mistress, Nui, is a local farmer's wife. After he sold her to Ushitora to settle a gambling debt, Ushitora gave her to Tokuemon as chattel to gain his support.
He learns from Silvanito that Ramón accused Julio of cheating during a card game and took Marisol as collateral.

beats.text: Then the same good deed, with the same hardness: he kills the guards, frees her, gives the family money and orders them to leave town at once. Leone adds one touch: the stranger wrecks the house to make it look like a Baxter attack.

source.quote: Sanjuro kills the guards and reunites the woman with her husband and son. He gives them some money and orders them to leave town immediately.

the Stranger kills the guards, frees Marisol, and wrecks the house where she was held to create the appearance of an attack by the Baxters. He gives money to Marisol and urges her family to leave town.

beats.text: And he gets caught.

Both times. Unosuke grows suspicious of Nui's escape and uncovers the betrayal; Sanjuro is beaten, imprisoned and tortured, then smuggled out of town in a coffin by Gonji, and recovers in a small temple near a cemetery. The Rojos discover who freed Marisol, capture and torture the stranger; Piripero, the coffin maker, gets him out in a coffin, and he recovers in an abandoned mine.

source.quote: Smuggled out of town in a coffin by Gonji
He then recuperates in a small temple near a cemetery.
With help from the local coffinmaker named Piripero, the Stranger escapes town by hiding in a coffin, and recuperates in an abandoned mine.

beats.text: And the return has the same trigger: the innkeeper. Gonji is captured by Ushitora; Silvanito is captured and tortured by the Rojos for the stranger's whereabouts.

source.quote: Upon learning that Gonji has been captured by Ushitora, Sanjuro returns to town
When Piripero tells him that Silvanito has been captured and tortured by the Rojos for the Stranger's whereabouts, he returns to town to confront them.

beats.text: So it is the same film with hats.

Not quite. Leone drops the official whose arrival stops the first battle, the mayor going mad, and the farmer's son who closes the story. He adds the massacre of a gold escort, the Baxter house burning with everyone inside, and the steel plate under the poncho.
What official? Tell me about the one Leone dropped.

A bugyō, a government official from Edo. Sanjuro has just set the two gangs against each other and expects a massacre; the official arrives, both sides retreat without a drop of blood, and the plan is foiled. He leaves to investigate the assassination of a fellow official in another town, and the assassins talking in Gonji's tavern hand Sanjuro his next lever: he captures them and sells them to Seibei.

source.quote: His plan is foiled due to the unexpected arrival of a bugyō (a government official), which prompts both Seibei and Ushitora to make a bloodless retreat.

The bugyō leaves soon after to investigate the assassination of a fellow official in another town. Overhearing the assassins discussing the hit in Gonji's tavern, Sanjuro later captures them and sells them to Seibei.

source.line: An inspector from Edo is coming!

beats.text: Leone replaces that whole mechanism with gold. The Rojos massacre a detachment of Mexican soldiers escorting a chest of gold to exchange for rifles; the stranger props two of the dead up at the cemetery and sells both families the story of two survivors.

source.quote: The Stranger witnesses the Rojos massacre a detachment of Mexican soldiers escorting a chest of gold (to exchange for rifles) and comes up with a plan. He takes two of the dead bodies to a nearby cemetery and props them up to make them appear alive.

source.line: Two of those soldiers got away. They are hiding out in the cemetery.

beats.text: And the endings differ in their last gestures. Sanjuro spares a terrified young man, the farmer's son from the opening, and sends him home; the deranged mayor Tazaemon comes out in a samurai outfit and stabs the brewer to death, and Sanjuro orders him to kill himself. Leone has Esteban aim at the stranger's back from a building, and Silvanito shoots him dead.

source.quote: He spares a terrified young man, the son of the elderly couple from the opening, and sends him back to his parents. As Sanjuro surveys the damage, a now deranged Tazaemon comes out of his home in a samurai outfit and stabs Tokuemon to death.
Esteban aims for the Stranger's back from a nearby building, but is shot dead by Silvanito.

beats.text: The steel plate. That is the scene everyone remembers.

And it is Leone's. In Yojimbo the duel is a pistol against a sword. Leone keeps the idea, Ramón's Winchester against a man who seems unarmed, and adds the armor. Ramón had said it himself: when you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.

source.line: When you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.

brick.caption: “When you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.” (00:58:26)

beats.text: Leave the plot. What does Leone do that Kurosawa doesn't?

Faces. The sheet calls it the first film to show Leone's style, influenced by John Ford's landscapes and by Kurosawa's method, and says he wanted an operatic feel: extreme close-ups functioning like arias in a traditional opera, lit with Renaissance-type lighting effects, portraits in their own right.

source.quote: This was influenced by both John Ford's cinematic landscaping and the Japanese method of direction honed by Akira Kurosawa.
so there are many examples of extreme closeups of the faces of different characters, functioning like arias in a traditional opera
often lit with Renaissance-type lighting effects

beats.text: The costume is Eastwood's own doing: black jeans from a sports shop on Hollywood Boulevard, the hat from a Santa Monica wardrobe firm, the cigars from a Beverly Hills store, the Colt, the gunbelt and the spurs brought from Rawhide, the poncho found in Spain. He does not smoke; the foul taste of the cigar put him in the right frame of mind. Leone: more than an actor, I needed a mask, and Eastwood, at that time, only had two expressions: with hat and no hat.

source.quote: He bought black jeans from a sports shop on Hollywood Boulevard; the hat came from a Santa Monica wardrobe firm; and the trademark cigars from a Beverly Hills store.
He also brought props from Rawhide, including a Cobra-handled Colt, a gunbelt and spurs. The poncho was acquired in Spain.
More than an actor, I needed a mask, and Eastwood, at that time, only had two expressions: with hat and no hat.

brick.text: More than an actor, I needed a mask.

beats.text: And the music? Everyone whistles that theme.

Ennio Morricone, credited as Dan Savio. Leone asked for a theme close to Dimitri Tiomkin's El Degüello from Rio Bravo; Morricone says he took a lullaby he had written before and developed it, and that the resemblance is in the execution, not the arrangement. Some of the music was written before the film, which Morricone calls unusual: Leone often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

source.quote: The film's music was written by Ennio Morricone, initially credited as Dan Savio.
Leone requested Morricone to write a theme that would be similar to Dimitri Tiomkin's El Degüello (used in Rio Bravo).
he often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

brick.text: He often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

beats.text: There is a quarrel here too. In 1962 the folk singer Peter Tevis had recorded Woody Guthrie's Pastures of Plenty in a Morricone arrangement; when the record was played at a meeting about the film, Leone said: that's it. Tevis claims the tune and the arrangements were copied for the opening title, Titoli.

source.quote: Leone said, "That's it", with Tevis claiming that the tune and musical arrangements were copied for the music for the opening title, "Titoli".

beats.text: On the other side, Masaru Sato, who said his main influence was Henry Mancini. Michael Wood, in the London Review of Books, hears drums, Japanese flutes mixed with American big band noises, jaunty and jangling throughout, discreetly off, as if half the band was playing in the wrong key; and he calls it the sound of Sanjuro's mind, discordant and undefeated and unserious.

source.quote: a loud, witty soundtrack by Masaru Sato, who said his main influence was Henry Mancini.
feels jaunty and jangling throughout, discreetly off, as if half the band was playing in the wrong key
the sound of his mind, discordant and undefeated and unserious

brick.text: The sound of his mind, discordant and undefeated and unserious.
brick.attribution: Michael Wood on Masaru Sato's score, London Review of Books

beats.text: Now the part I do not get. Kurosawa says it is my film. Where did Kurosawa get it?
From Dashiell Hammett, by his own account: he named The Glass Key, the 1942 film noir made from Hammett's 1931 novel.

source.quote: Kurosawa stated that a major source for the plot was the 1942 film noir classic The Glass Key, an adaptation of Dashiell Hammett's 1931 novel of the same name.

beats.text: But the database links Yojimbo to another Hammett novel, Red Harvest: a nameless detective in a mining town run by rival gangs, setting them against each other. And the text is careful. Desser and Farber say Red Harvest was the inspiration; Donald Richie calls the resemblance coincidental.

source.quote: Kurosawa scholar David Desser, and film critic Manny Farber claim that Red Harvest was the inspiration for the film; however, Donald Richie and other scholars believe the similarities are coincidental.

beats.text: Tell me about that novel, then. I only know the title.

Red Harvest, 1929, serialized first in the pulp magazine Black Mask from November 1927, starting with an installment called The Cleansing of Poisonville. The narrator is the Continental Op, drawn from Hammett's own years as a Pinkerton operative. He is called to Personville, Poisonville to the locals, a Montana mining town taken over by gangs after a labor dispute; some of it comes from the Anaconda Road massacre of 1920 in Butte.

source.quote: Red Harvest is a 1929 novel by American writer Dashiell Hammett.
much of which is drawn from his own experiences as an operative of the Pinkerton Detective Agency
Some of the novel was inspired by the Anaconda Road massacre, a 1920 labor dispute in the mining town of Butte, Montana.
Part 1: "The Cleansing of Poisonville", Black Mask, November 1927

brick.caption: Black Mask, November 1927: The Cleansing of Poisonville

beats.text: The Op does what Sanjuro will do. He extracts information and leaks it to the warring parties, a gang war erupts, and the book shows him disturbed by the slaughter he orchestrated, drinking into a blackout and waking next to a woman stabbed with the ice pick he had handled. Time put the book among the hundred best English-language novels since 1923; André Gide called it the last word in atrocity, cynicism, and horror.

source.quote: The Op extracts information from Brand and Noonan, and increases tension in the city by leaking it to the warring parties.
The Op, disturbed by the slaughter he orchestrated, spends an evening of blackout inebriation with Brand
Time included Red Harvest in its 100 Best English-Language Novels from 1923 to 2005
a remarkable achievement, the last word in atrocity, cynicism, and horror

brick.text: The last word in atrocity, cynicism, and horror.

beats.text: And it kept breeding. The Coen brothers took the title of Blood Simple from a line of the Op, and Miller's Crossing borrows from it too. Rian Johnson's Brick was inspired by Hammett, this novel in particular. Donald Westlake wrote a screenplay that was never produced; and as of 2024, Scott Frank and Megan Abbott are writing a script for A24.

source.quote: The Coen brothers' film Blood Simple (1984) takes its title from a line in Red Harvest
The dialogue and plot of director Rian Johnson's debut feature, Brick, was inspired by the novels of Dashiell Hammett, particularly Red Harvest.
Donald E. Westlake wrote an unproduced screenplay adapting Red Harvest
As of 2024, Scott Frank and Megan Abbott are writing a script for Red Harvest for A24.

beats.text: So nobody has filmed the book itself.
Nobody, in nearly a century. Two films that may descend from it, a Walter Hill film in which critics find its elements, and the novel still waiting.

source.quote: Critics have noted elements of Red Harvest in the 1996 Walter Hill film Last Man Standing

beats.text: So the database says yes and the page says maybe.
Both are true. The graph records the lineage, the text records the argument about it. You get both.

Leone used exactly that. His defense named three sources: Yojimbo, Red Harvest, and most of all Goldoni's play, Servant of Two Masters, a man playing two camps against each other, which rooted the story in Italian culture. And then: Kurosawa's Yojimbo was inspired by an American novel of the series-noire so I was really taking the story back home again.

source.quote: Partly derived from Kurosawa's samurai film Yojimbo, partly from Dashiell Hammett's novel Red Harvest (1929), but most of all from Carlo Goldoni's eighteenth-century play Servant of Two Masters [sic].
Kurosawa's Yojimbo was inspired by an American novel of the series-noire so I was really taking the story back home again.

brick.text: I was really taking the story back home again.

beats.text: He had other alibis in the frame: the sheet notes that Leone also referenced American Westerns in the film, most notably Shane and My Darling Clementine, both of which differ from Yojimbo.

source.quote: Leone also referenced numerous American Westerns in the film, most notably Shane and My Darling Clementine, both of which differ from Yojimbo.

beats.text: Cheeky. Give me one line that is pure Leone, then.
The mule. Fourteen minutes in, after the Baxter men have shot at his mule and laughed, the stranger walks back: you see, my mule don't like people laughing. There is no mule in Yojimbo.

source.line: You see, my mule don't like people laughing.

brick.caption: “You see, my mule don't like people laughing.” (00:14:53)

beats.text: Did Eastwood know what he was getting into?

Better than anyone. Years earlier, in a Los Angeles theater on Western Avenue, he had watched Yojimbo thinking it would make a great western if only someone had nerve enough to do it. When the script reached him, about five or ten pages in he recognized it as an obvious rip-off of Yojimbo. He found that ironic.

source.quote: A few years later, after someone handed him the script for A Fistful of Dollars, "about five or 10 pages in" he "recognized it as an obvious rip-off" of Yojimbo, which he found ironic.

beats.text: Was he even the first choice?

Far from it. Leone wanted Henry Fonda; the production could not afford a major Hollywood star. Charles Bronson declined and said the script was bad. Henry Silva, Rory Calhoun, Tony Russel, Steve Reeves, Ty Hardin and James Coburn all turned it down; Coburn was the one Leone wanted, and he was too expensive. Fonda and Bronson would both star in Once Upon a Time in the West.

source.quote: Originally, Sergio Leone intended Henry Fonda to play the "Man with No Name". However, the production company could not afford to employ a major Hollywood star. Next, Leone offered the part to Charles Bronson. He, too, declined, saying that the script was bad.
Other actors who turned down the role were Henry Silva, Rory Calhoun, Tony Russel, Steve Reeves, Ty Hardin and James Coburn. Leone said he wanted Coburn for the role, but he was deemed too expensive.

beats.text: Then Richard Harrison, an American living in Italy who had just made Gunfight at Red Sands, refused too; when the producers showed him a list of lesser-known Americans, he pointed at Eastwood, who could play a cowboy convincingly. Harrison later said: maybe my greatest contribution to cinema was not doing A Fistful of Dollars and recommending Clint for the part. Eastwood's own reason: in Rawhide, he had got awfully tired of playing the conventional white hat, and decided it was time to be an antihero.

source.quote: Maybe my greatest contribution to cinema was not doing A Fistful of Dollars and recommending Clint for the part.
I decided it was time to be an antihero.

brick.text: Maybe my greatest contribution to cinema was not doing A Fistful of Dollars and recommending Clint for the part.

beats.text: An Italian crew, an American lead. How did they even talk?

Barely. Leone did not speak English; Eastwood went through the actor and stuntman Benito Stefanelli, an uncredited interpreter who later appeared in Leone's other pictures. Like other Italian films of the time, everything was shot silent and dubbed afterwards. In the Italian version Eastwood is dubbed by Enrico Maria Salerno, whose sinister rendition contrasts with Eastwood's cocksure and darkly humorous interpretation.

source.quote: Leone did not speak English and Eastwood communicated with the Italian cast and crew mostly through the actor and stuntman Benito Stefanelli
all footage was filmed silent, and the dialogue and sound effects were dubbed in post-production

For the Italian version of the film, Eastwood was dubbed by the actor Enrico Maria Salerno, whose sinister rendition of the Man with No Name's voice contrasted with Eastwood's cocksure and darkly humorous interpretation.

beats.text: And Mifune? Any stories?

One. After Kurosawa scolded him for arriving late one morning, Mifune made a point of being on set at six every day, in full makeup and costume, for the rest of the shoot. The sword choreography came from Yoshio Sugino of the Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū, and the cinematographer was Kazuo Miyagawa, Kurosawa's second film with him after Rashomon.

source.quote: After Kurosawa scolded Mifune for arriving late to the set one morning, Mifune made it a point to be ready on set at 6:00 a.m. every day in full makeup and costume for the rest of the film's shooting schedule.
This was the second film where director Akira Kurosawa worked with cinematographer Kazuo Miyagawa (the first being Rashomon in 1950).
The sword instruction and choreography for the film were done by Yoshio Sugino of the Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū and Ryū Kuze.

brick.caption: Mifune, on set at six every morning

beats.text: And who actually wrote it?

Nobody agrees. The historian Roberto Curti calls the accounts contradictory and difficult to decipher: Valerii, Bolzoni, Tessari, Di Leo each claim a share, and Leone suggested he wrote the whole screenplay himself. The working title was Il Magnifico Straniero, the magnificent stranger.
And when the Americans finally saw it?

Late. Distributors feared being sued by Kurosawa, so it reached American cinemas on the eighteenth of January 1967. Bosley Crowther, in the New York Times, called Eastwood a morbid, amusing, campy fraud. Philip French found the film totally devoid of human feeling.

source.quote: The release of the film was delayed in the United States, because distributors feared being sued by Kurosawa. As a result, it was not shown in American cinemas until 18 January 1967.
He is a morbid, amusing, campy fraud.
A Fistful of Dollars looks awful, has a flat dead soundtrack, and is totally devoid of human feeling.

brick.text: He is a morbid, amusing, campy fraud.
brick.attribution: Bosley Crowther, The New York Times, 1967

beats.text: Not everyone. Variety praised a James Bondian vigor and tongue-in-cheek approach that was sure to capture both sophisticates and average cinema patrons.

source.quote: a James Bondian vigor and tongue-in-cheek approach that was sure to capture both sophisticates and average cinema patrons

beats.text: Television wanted it tamer. For the ABC broadcast of the twenty-third of February 1975, a four-and-a-half-minute prologue was added to contextualize the character and justify the violence: written and directed by Monte Hellman, with Harry Dean Stanton as an unidentified U.S. official offering the imprisoned Man With No Name a pardon in exchange for cleaning up San Miguel, Eastwood's close-ups cut in from archival footage. It opened television showings for a few years, disappeared, and came back on the Special Edition DVD and the Blu-ray.

source.quote: a four-and-a-half-minute prologue was added to the film to contextualize the character and justify the violence. Written and directed by Monte Hellman, it featured an unidentified U.S. official (Harry Dean Stanton) offering the imprisoned Man With No Name a chance at a pardon in exchange for cleaning up San Miguel.
This prologue opened television presentations for a few years before disappearing; it reappeared on the Special Edition DVD and the more recent Blu-ray

beats.text: And Yojimbo, how did America take that one?

With a bathroom. A 1968 screening in the planned community of Columbia, Maryland was considered too violent for viewers, and the hosts hid in the bathroom to avoid the audience. Elsewhere it did fine: an Academy Award nomination for costume design, the Volpi Cup for Mifune at Venice, Japan's fourth highest-grossing film of 1961, and Pauline Kael calling it Kurosawa's first shaggy man movie, a farce of force.

source.quote: A 1968 screening in the planned community of Columbia, Maryland was considered too violent for viewers, causing the hosts to hide in the bathroom to avoid the audience.
Yojimbo was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Costume Design at the 34th Academy Awards. Toshiro Mifune won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor at the 22nd Venice Film Festival.
Yojimbo was Japan's fourth highest-grossing film of 1961
Pauline Kael described the film as Kurosawa's "first shaggy man" movie going on to call it a wonderful satire-comedy and "farce of force."

beats.text: Time reversed the verdicts. Fistful stands at 98 percent on Rotten Tomatoes, and the 67th Cannes Film Festival, in 2014, celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of the birth of the spaghetti Western by showing it. Yojimbo sits at 96 percent, 93 on Metacritic, number 23 on Kinema Junpo's list of the greatest Japanese films, and number 95 in Empire's 500.

source.quote: A Fistful of Dollars has achieved a 98% approval rating from 55 critical reviews on Rotten Tomatoes
The 67th Cannes Film Festival, held in 2014, celebrated the
96% of 50 critics' reviews are positive
Metacritic, which uses a weighted average, assigned the film a score of 93 out of 100

In 2009 the film was voted at No. 23 on the list of The Greatest Japanese Films of All Time by Japanese film magazine Kinema Junpo. Yojimbo was also ranked at #95 in Empire magazine's list of the 500 Greatest Films of All Time.

beats.text: Ouch. Did anyone learn the lesson?
Three decades later. Last Man Standing, Walter Hill's 1996 remake with Bruce Willis, is official: Kurosawa and Kikushima are in its credits for the original story.

source.quote: Last Man Standing (1996), a Prohibition-era action film directed by Walter Hill and starring Bruce Willis, is an official remake of Yojimbo: both Kikushima and Kurosawa specifically listed in this movie's credits as having provided the original story.

beats.text: The family is larger. Django, 1966, Sergio Corbucci, Franco Nero in the title role, a looser adaptation. The Warrior and the Sorceress, 1984, a sword and sorcery take. Inferno, 1999, also called Desert Heat. Michael G. Wilson compared Licence to Kill to Yojimbo: Bond sows the seeds of distrust until the villain brings himself down. Lawrence Kasdan said his inspiration for The Bodyguard was Yojimbo with Steve McQueen as the lead. And the writers of the first season of Barry found they had, in their words, kinda just did Yojimbo, and said so in the show.

source.quote: A second, looser western adaptation, Django (1966), was directed by Sergio Corbucci and featured Franco Nero in the title role.
Other retellings include The Warrior and the Sorceress (1984), a sword and sorcery take, and Inferno (1999, aka Desert Heat).
only sowing the seeds of distrust, he manages to have the villain bring himself down
Yojimbo with Steve McQueen as the lead.

beats.text: And the homages: Star Wars, A New Hope and The Last Jedi, Samurai Jack, Usagi Yojimbo. Mifune's character became the model for John Belushi's Samurai Futaba on Saturday Night Live, and Roger Clark cited Yojimbo for his Arthur Morgan in Red Dead Redemption 2. Kurosawa himself came back the next year with Sanjuro, where the man names himself after camellia bushes, as he had after mulberry trees.

source.quote: Other works that pay narrative and visual homage to Yojimbo include Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope (1977), Star Wars: The Last Jedi (2017), Samurai Jack (2002) and Usagi Yojimbo.

And the loop closes on Eastwood. In the early 1970s Bertolucci prepared his own Red Harvest, and for the detective he considered Redford, Nicholson, and Clint Eastwood, who had played the Op-inspired Man with No Name. It was never made.

source.quote: For the role of the Op he considered Robert Redford, Jack Nicholson (who had played a hard-boiled detective in Roman Polanski's neo-noir film Chinatown), and Clint Eastwood (who had played the Op-inspired "Man with No Name" in Sergio Leone's Dollars Trilogy).
